CANBERRA, June 17, 2024 — Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Chinese Premier Li Qiang held talks in Canberra on Monday, seeking to stabilise relations after years of trade disputes while acknowledging differences over security.

Li's four-day trip was the first visit to Australia by a Chinese premier since 2017. It followed Albanese's visit to Beijing in November 2023, part of a diplomatic thaw between Australia and its largest trading partner.

Albanese said the discussions covered trade, regional security and human rights. Li announced that China would include Australia in its visa-waiver programme, a step aimed at encouraging travel and business links.

Relations deteriorated sharply in 2020 after Australia called for an independent inquiry into the origins of COVID-19. China subsequently imposed tariffs and other restrictions on a range of Australian exports.

Beijing removed duties on Australian barley in August 2023 and wine in March 2024, reopening important markets. Restrictions affecting Australian rock lobster remained unresolved at the time of the Canberra talks.

The rapprochement has not erased strategic tensions. Australia has criticised China's conduct in the South China Sea and is pursuing nuclear-powered submarines under the AUKUS partnership with the United States and Britain, an arrangement Beijing opposes.

Li began his visit in Adelaide, where he said China would provide a new pair of giant pandas to replace the pair at the city's zoo.

Australia, Tuvalu sign climate migration and security pact

CANBERRA, Nov. 10, 2023 — Australia and Tuvalu signed a treaty on Friday offering citizens of the low-lying Pacific island nation a pathway to live in Australia as rising seas threaten their homeland, while strengthening security ties between the two countries.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Tuvalu Prime Minister Kausea Natano announced the Falepili Union treaty at the Pacific Islands Forum leaders’ meeting in the Cook Islands.

Australia said it would initially offer places to up to 280 Tuvaluans a year under a special pathway allowing them to live, work and study in Australia. Tuvalu has a population of about 11,000.

The agreement recognises Tuvalu’s continuing statehood and sovereignty even if climate change causes the loss of its physical territory. Its low-lying atolls are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and coastal flooding.

Under the treaty, Australia commits to assist Tuvalu, at its request, in response to a major natural disaster, a public health emergency or military aggression.

Tuvalu, in turn, must mutually agree with Australia on any partnership or arrangement with another country concerning security and defence. The provision covers areas including policing, border protection and critical infrastructure.

The pact comes amid competition for influence in the Pacific between China and the United States and its allies. Beijing’s 2022 security agreement with the Solomon Islands heightened concern in Canberra and Washington over China’s expanding regional role.

The treaty requires domestic approval processes before entering into force.
